analysis.body:
Per the Census Bureau, 24.7% of health care and social assistance firms (NAICS 62) reported using AI in the last two weeks, up from 24.0% in the prior period. The question was first asked in September 2023. This is the measured adoption baseline for the sector.

Per WHO, AI holds promise for diagnosis, treatment, health research, drug development, and public health functions including surveillance and outbreak response. Per NIH, the agency makes biomedical data findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable, and aims to make electronic health record, omics, imaging, and disease-specific data usable with AI and machine learning applications. The Medical Models catalog on this site tracks the 1,000 most-downloaded open medical models on the Hugging Face Hub, refreshed daily, covering clinical and imaging models.

Vendor and capital tracking is split across several sources. Per KLAS, its research comes from candid feedback from healthcare executives, physicians, nurses, IT professionals, and administrators, and its annual Best in KLAS report recognizes software and services companies that help healthcare organizations accomplish the Quadruple Aim. Per Rock Health, it publishes widely cited research on digital health funding and special topics. Per Artificial Analysis, which ranks models on medical tasks, independent benchmarks compare AI models and API hosting providers across quality, price, output speed, and latency, with model providers including Anthropic, OpenAI, Meta, Google, DeepSeek, and Mistral, and hosting endpoints from Amazon, Azure, Google Vertex, CoreWeave, and Together AI.

The clearest quantitative evidence in these sources is model performance and cost, not provider-level return on investment. Per OpenAI, HealthBench was built with 262 physicians from 60 countries and includes 5,000 realistic health conversations with 48,562 unique rubric criteria across seven themes. OpenAI reports that o3 outperforms Claude 3.7 Sonnet and Gemini 2.5 Pro (Mar 2025), that its frontier models improved by 28% on HealthBench, and that GPT-4.1 nano outperforms August 2024's GPT-4o despite being 25x cheaper. OpenAI also notes that a single unsafe or incorrect answer can outweigh the benefit of many good ones, and that worst-of-n reliability has improved but significant room remains.

Governance and risk are addressed at the international and federal levels. Per WHO, the guidance on ethics and governance of AI for health identifies ethical challenges and risks, sets six consensus principles, and includes recommendations to hold public and private stakeholders accountable, with ethics and human rights at the heart of design, deployment, and use. Per NIH, policies, guidelines, and best practices should be considered as investigators pursue development and use of AI in biomedical and behavioral research.

A reader deciding whether to deploy AI in healthcare should weigh the measured adoption of 24.7% against the available infrastructure and guardrails. The sources collectively provide a governance frame from WHO, data infrastructure and policy from NIH, vendor feedback through KLAS, capital tracking through Rock Health, and model benchmarks through HealthBench and Artificial Analysis. The evidence shows improving model capability and cost, but reliability gaps remain, and the WHO ethics principles and NIH guidelines are the reference points for deployment.

https://klasresearch.com/.brief: KLAS Research is a community that brings together healthcare leaders, IT professionals, and vendors to share candid provider feedback and collaborate on best practices. The organization gathers insights directly from thousands of healthcare professionals, executives, physicians, nurses, IT staff, and administrators, who use IT solutions and services, and uses that feedback to produce market reports and live data. Its annual Best in KLAS report ranks software and services companies that help healthcare organizations achieve the Quadruple Aim, based on year-long feedback from provider and payer professionals. Since 1996, KLAS has aimed to improve healthcare by amplifying provider and payer voices and expanding its research scope to meet evolving technology needs.

https://artificialanalysis.ai/.brief: Artificial Analysis offers independent benchmarks comparing AI models and API hosting providers across quality, price, output speed, and latency. The page indicates whether model weights are available and labels models as commercial-use restricted or non-commercial depending on license conditions. Its AA-AnalystAgent benchmark reports the share of questions answered correctly on all five attempts, which the site describes as measuring reliability rather than occasional correctness. The page also lists the cost to run evaluations in its Intelligence Index and the tokens per second received during generation. For provider endpoints, it presents a composite score showing how much of a model’s accuracy is preserved, expressed as a percentage of a reference endpoint.

https://rockhealth.com/insights/.brief: The page says it publishes perspectives on trends shaping the future of healthcare. It notes that its work is at the forefront of digital health. Readers are invited to browse its research on digital health funding and special topics in the healthcare industry. The research is described as “widely-cited.”

https://openai.com/index/healthbench/.brief: HealthBench is a new benchmark for AI in healthcare that evaluates models in realistic scenarios, built with input from 262 physicians across 60 countries. It contains 5,000 “realistic health conversations,” each graded by a physician-written rubric with 48,562 unique criteria, and responses are scored by a GPT-4.1 grader. OpenAI reports that its frontier models, such as o3, have outperformed others and improved by 28% on HealthBench, while a small GPT-4.1 nano model now outperforms the older GPT-4o at 25× lower cost. The benchmark also includes a “HealthBench Hard” subset of 1,000 difficult examples and tracks worst-of-n reliability curves, showing room for further gains.

https://datascience.nih.gov/artificial-i.brief: NIH reports that it makes a wealth of biomedical data available to research communities. It aims to make these data “findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable, or FAIR” and usable with AI/ML applications. NIH notes that its unique data types, electronic health records, omics, imaging, disease-specific data, create opportunities for novel AI/ML approaches. The agency also emphasizes establishing partnerships and providing policies, guidelines, and best practices for investigators using AI in biomedical and behavioral research, and references Data Management Frameworks.

https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/.brief: The WHO report on ethics and governance of AI for health outlines the ethical challenges and risks of using AI in healthcare and presents six consensus principles to ensure AI benefits all countries. It was developed over eighteen months by experts in ethics, digital technology, law, human rights, and ministries of health. The guidance stresses that AI technologies, which can improve diagnosis, treatment, research, drug development, and support public health functions such as surveillance and outbreak response, must center ethics and human rights in their design, deployment, and use. It also offers recommendations to hold public and private stakeholders accountable and responsive to healthcare workers and affected communities.

https://theworldofai.org/ai-ecosystem/te.brief: The page lists the 1000 most-downloaded open medical models on the Hugging Face Hub, showing each model’s licence, download count, and release date, and it updates this information daily. It also mentions books by Stephen R. Jordan, including the “The Operating Discipline for AI Library™” series, now available on Amazon. Additionally, the page enumerates a range of AI audit and assessment services such as The AI Business Enablement Audit™, The AI Readiness & Performance Assessment™, The AI Risk & Governance Review™, The AI Efficiency & Process Optimization™, The AI IT Security Audit™, The AI IT Security Implementation & Strategy™, Secure by Design in the Age of AI™, Application Security in the Age of AI™, and The AI Lawyer.
